item.title: Reuse of cast-in-place concrete: overcoming industry barriers
item.description:
Mainstreaming the reuse of elements extracted from cast-in-place (CIP) reinforced concrete (RC) structures beyond pilot projects requires more than environmental motivation: it requires resolving technical, logistical, contractual and institutional barriers. Research has so far centred on prefabricated systems, leaving CIP structures only partially addressed. The latter are monolithic: recovering elements requires saw-cutting, and every transaction currently demands bespoke negotiation between donor and receiving projects. This bilateral matching does not scale. A systemic analysis is presented of three recent Swiss deconstruction case studies. Four categories of barriers are identified that together prevent the formation of an industrial reuse market. Drawing on a steel-section analogy and a synthesis of systemic interdependencies, three conditions are formulated for creating a viable market for CIP reuse involving a decoupling of supply and demand (a normalised dimensional grid, versatile connection systems, and a stock-holding and guarantee function). Elements would therefore be cut and stocked before any receiver is identified. Standardising element dimensions proves limiting for a heterogeneous stock and a small demolition flow. A set of more versatile connection details would reduce costs and enhance the reuse of CIP elements.

PRACTICE RELEVANCE

To mainstream CIP concrete reuse beyond pilot projects, three changes in industry practice are immediately actionable. First, pre-demolition reusability assessments with standardised factsheets should become routine inputs to design, reframing the engineer’s role from a specifier of new products to a characteriser of an existing material stock. Second, template donor–receiver contracts allocating liability, custody and inspection should replace case-by-case negotiation. Third, the design community should converge toward a versatile family of connection details (timber, steel or concrete substructures accepting a range of element dimensions), so that elements from different donor structures remain interchangeable with each other and with new slabs. The Simplon case (CHF128/m², about €137/m², for extraction alone versus CHF200/m², about €213/m², for an equivalent new slab) indicates that extraction is economically viable. What remains is the value-chain reorganisation that downstream coordination requires.

item.title: Timing matters: life cycle embodied GHG emissions of circular building strategies
item.description:
Circular building strategies (CBS) aim to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions related to the construction, maintenance and end-of-life of buildings. However, the timing of these reductions, whether immediate or in the future, is often overlooked. Given the urgency of addressing climate change, accounting for the temporal dimension is crucial to understand accurately the decarbonisation effects of CBS. Existing life cycle assessment (LCA) studies on CBS are analysed for the timing of reported reductions and the connected temporal considerations in the model. The analysis of LCA studies (n = 42) shows consistent reduction patterns for upstream CBS (e.g. reuse of existing components), but the assessment model includes little temporal detail. The reductions are more inconclusive for downstream CBS (e.g. design for disassembly), and they highly depend on temporal modelling. The findings highlight the need for a consistent LCA framework that accounts for the timing of GHG emission reductions when applying CBS. The identification of when actual GHG reductions occur arising from different circular strategies will aid in the understanding of CBS’s role in meeting climate targets.

POLICY RELEVANCE

CBS do not deliver GHG emission reductions equally over time, which has direct implications for policy design and decision-making. CBS acting early in the life cycle (e.g. component reuse) consistently reduce upfront emissions, supporting near-term climate targets. However, downstream CBS (e.g. design for disassembly) produce uncertain or delayed benefits, limiting their effectiveness for urgent decarbonisation goals. Current assessment methods often overlook this temporal dimension, risking misaligned incentives. LCA frameworks should be updated to explicitly report and account for when GHG emissions occur, not just the overall reduction. Additionally, policy frameworks should differentiate between short- and long-term mitigation, aligning subsidies, GHG emission limits, and reporting standards accordingly. Recommendations are provided to support evidence-based decisions and ensure the building sector contributes effectively to near- and long-term climate targets.

item.title: Scaling up retrofit: regional challenges and opportunities for MMC
item.description:
Increasing energy retrofit rates is considered essential for reducing housing-related greenhouse gas emissions, particularly in Central and Northern Europe. In Germany, despite ambitious and costly policies, annual retrofit rates have remained largely stagnant at around 1% of the housing stock. The current trend of modern methods of construction (MMC) and digitisation have renewed hope that serial retrofit and service platforms could enable the scaling up of energy retrofits by reducing costs, disruptions and management burdens, especially for non-professional property owners. While a growing literature explores this potential, empirical research on the region-specific conditions to scale up serial retrofit remains limited. To address this gap, this study interviewed intermediaries and professionals who organise retrofits in the Freiburg region in south-west Germany. Their views were sought on the challenges and opportunities for serial (prefabricated) retrofit facilitated by digitised planning, platform thinking, and collaboration among trades and other partners. Applying the challenge-oriented regional innovation systems (CORIS) framework revealed an early-stage reorientation pathway in the region, providing entry points for scaling up MMC.

PRACTICE RELEVANCE

There is leeway for practitioners to deepen existing and create new networks across sectors and trades, and to experiment with collaborative methods, working towards serial approaches. The early adoption of innovative methods and the use of regional and renewable resources is recommended to strengthen both ecological sustainability and the regional economy. As for governance, the provision of digital tools and legal bases for data collection is essential to promote a transformation pathway for MMC and platforms. Institutional innovations such as publicly funded one-stop shops and database can contribute to a comprehensive housing transition.

item.title: Indoor temperature and office work performance in a temperate climate
item.description:
The relationship between indoor temperature and office work performance (OWP) remains contested. Previous laboratory studies, including a controlled experiment in Singapore, report limited or no effects within typical office ranges, but replication across climatic contexts is needed to assess generalizability. The present study was conducted in the temperate climate of the San Francisco Bay Area, closely replicating the Singapore protocol with a 30% larger sample: 75 participants completed four 165-min sessions at 21, 23, 25, and 27°C in a controlled environmental chamber. OWP was assessed using the Cognitive Ability Test (CAT) and a battery of eight neuropsychological tests targeting five cognitive domains, alongside continuous physiological monitoring. Although participants preferred temperatures between 23 and 25°C, no statistically significant effect of temperature on cognitive ability or neuropsychological performance was found across the full sample; physiological measures and thermal perception varied with temperature as expected, but without accompanying changes in OWP. Among the highest-performing quartile of CAT participants, a statistically significant, large-magnitude temperature-related effect was observed, though this pattern was not replicated in the neuropsychological battery. The findings closely align with the Singapore study and are consistent with the Maximal Adaptability Model, supporting wider heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) setpoint ranges.

PRACTICE RELEVANCE

Building managers, HVAC engineers, and sustainability practitioners face increasing pressure to reduce energy consumption from heating and cooling while maintaining occupant work performance. This study provides experimental evidence that OWP was not significantly impaired across a 21–27°C range in a temperate climate (San Francisco Bay Area). These findings suggest that modest upward adjustments to HVAC cooling setpoints within this range are unlikely to reduce cognitive output in typical office populations, supporting strategies that expand acceptable indoor temperature bands as a means of reducing energy usage. Decision-makers should note that thermal comfort and satisfaction remain important even when performance is stable, and that these results are most applicable to temperate-climate offices with predominantly young, healthy workers performing structured task work. Longer duration exposure and more diverse occupant profiles warrant further investigation.

item.title: Moving homes and energy poverty: residents’ concerns, capabilities and responses
item.description:
In the study of energy poverty and vulnerability, limited attention has been paid to the social differentiation and unequal capacities to act. This study examined housing mobility as part of energy action space, asking how the possibility, or impossibility, of moving home shapes energy vulnerability. In-depth interviews (n = 29) conducted during 2024 and 2025 with Finnish residents of detached houses investigated how moving home is discussed after the rapid rise in energy prices in 2022. Some households experience a lock-in beyond their control and inability to move, resulting in aggravated concern for the energy costs and living conditions in their house. Whilst moving home might be a form of effective energy action, it is difficult due to financial constraints, health, housing market conditions or emotional attachment. Moving home also requires capacities of anticipation and timely action. Housing immobility forms a layer of vulnerability that coexists with other forms of vulnerability. The findings challenge the assumption that owner-occupants of detached houses do not experience energy poverty due to their asset ownership.

POLICY RELEVANCE

Energy policy instruments that focus narrowly on prices or on energy efficiency risk overlooking how energy vulnerability is produced through housing trajectories and immobility. Particularly in contexts where home ownership is widespread, policies need to consider the barriers of moving homes and relocating. Public authorities need to consider how housing development, renovation support and mobility options shape the energy action space. Policy should support not only energy retrofits but also feasible housing alternatives and options that allow households to move before their vulnerability becomes entrenched. In more general terms, recognising that people may move home because of high energy costs and poor energy efficiency can help to support market developments towards energy retrofits, not only in the stock of owner-occupied detached houses but also in the rental market, in which property owners need to retrofit to keep their assets attractive.

item.title: Reference study for biogenic carbon storage in the residential building stock
item.description:
The built environment is both a major source of greenhouse gas emissions and an important area for climate mitigation through material choices, design and long-term use. Wood products can reduce emissions by substituting more carbon-intensive construction materials while also storing biogenic carbon in buildings. However, these benefits depend on how long buildings remain in use and how much carbon they retain over time. This study examines residential buildings in Helsinki, Finland, to estimate observed stock survival, quantify cumulative biogenic carbon storage in the residential building stock, and compare the results with estimates based on replacement cycles and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC) default 35-year half-life for harvested wood products (HWP). Results indicate high residential stock survival, with 92% of floor area still in use from the earliest study periods (1921–39). Timber buildings account for 40% of total biogenic carbon storage, despite representing only 10% of the gross floor area (GFA). The existing stock stores an estimated 266–285 kt C compared with 123 kt C predicted by the IPCC’s default half-life estimation. The results show that the IPCC’s default decay assumption produces substantially lower estimates when applied to long-lived residential building components.

POLICY RELEVANCE

This study provides empirical evidence on the survival of residential buildings and the associated long-term storage of biogenic carbon in wood materials. Helsinki’s existing residential stock stores approximately 266–285 kt C, indicating that long-lived buildings form a relevant urban carbon stock. The results also show that residential building survival is shaped not only by materials but also by stable housing demand as well as by institutional factors such as planning regulations, zoning, renovation programmes and heritage protection. For policymakers, better empirical data on building survival and component replacement can improve assumptions used in whole-life carbon assessment and evaluations of wood use in construction. The comparison with the IPCC’s default 35-year half-life further shows the importance of distinguishing broad HWP accounting assumptions from the behaviour of long-lived wood products in residential buildings.

item.title: Building space heating and cooling in NDCs 4.0
item.description:
Calls and initiatives for incorporating the building stock into Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement indicate the large potential to mitigate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. With the update of NDC 4.0 for 2030, the opportunity exists to include national building stocks as an action area in NDC 4.0. Worldwide, the GHG emissions caused by national building stocks are dominated by energy consumption for the operation of buildings, especially for heating and cooling. In the Global North, the expenditure of energy and GHG emissions for heating must be further drastically reduced. Worldwide, and especially in the Global South, it is a matter of limiting the increase in mechanical cooling (i.e. air-conditioning) demand by finding a compromise with the safeguarding of thermal comfort. The first step is to account for the GHG emissions associated with space heating and cooling, including emissions from the electricity and district heating used in buildings. This briefing note argues that including space heating and cooling in NDC 4.0 is feasible and desirable and it proposes a staged approach for policymakers.

ACTION POINTS

  • The built environment can provide a large contribution to achieving individual national targets for reducing energy consumption and limiting GHG emissions. There is potential for all countries to include the built environment in their NDCs and national mitigation strategies.
  • A first step is the examination of energy consumption and GHG emissions of residential and non-residential buildings, caused by space heating and cooling during their operation.
  • To identify opportunities for reducing GHG emissions, countries should assess SCOPE 1 emissions from fuels used in buildings and SCOPE 2 emissions associated with the electricity and district heating or cooling they consume. This end-use assessment can complement national emissions inventories.

item.title: Building component reuse as sociomaterial interaction: lessons from precast concrete
item.description:
Building component reuse (BCR) has become a promising strategy for the construction sector to move towards sustainability transformation. Although earlier studies on the construction sector have characterised material flows as dynamic human–material interactions, the ways materials become valuable and exceed human control remain underexamined in the context of BCR. This study examines BCR through sociomateriality and explores the different manifestations of sociomaterial interactions in BCR. The study presents a qualitative single-case study on precast concrete element reuse in Finland, utilising 19 semi-structured interviews, 58 months of ethnographic observations, and secondary data gathered between 2021 and 2026. Eight sociomaterial interaction types—‘Compliance’, ‘Human orientation’, ‘Interpretative framing’, ‘Leverage’, ‘Proof of concept’, ‘Advocate for material’, ‘Exaptation’ and ‘Uncertain business environment’—are identified in which reused building components can manifest in two different ways: as an intermediary or as a carrier. To be successful, BCR needs to be addressed as a broad phenomenon rather than as a mere techno-economic management issue if meaningful sustainability transformation of the construction sector is to be promoted. The findings serve as recognised intervention points for facilitating the mainstreaming of BCR and the sustainability transformation of the construction sector in general.

PRACTICE RELEVANCE

Insights are provided for practitioners and policymakers to promote BCR. The study identifies eight sociomaterial interaction types that serve as recognised intervention points to facilitate the mainstreaming of BCR. This depends on both organisational interactions amongst multiple actors and technical requirements involving institutional conditions, demands and expectations. Accordingly, eight practical recommendations are suggested for practitioners and regulators that can be harnessed to mainstream of BCR. Public actors in regulation, procurement practices and circular construction policies can adapt technical requirements, institutional conditions, demand structures and shared expectations that shape construction activities.

item.title: Validating national reuse indicators from regional demolition data: a Swedish example
item.description:
Construction accounts for a substantial share of global emissions and waste, highlighting the need to shift from linear to circular resource flows and to prioritise deconstruction and reuse over demolition and disposal. Enabling this transition requires reliable methods for identifying and quantifying products embedded in existing buildings. This Swedish study examines whether key performance indicators (KPIs) derived from demolition‑permit documentation can be generalised across regions to support product‑level stock estimation for circular construction. Using a bottom‑up method, regional similarities and differences were assessed using data on product quantities from preschool and multifamily‑building demolitions (n = 38) in Umeå and Stockholm. Six product categories were compiled from demolition permits and compared statistically with Greater Gothenburg values. The results show that while several products exhibit modest regional variation, others—gypsum boards and clay roof tiles in preschools, and wooden windows in multifamily buildings—display statistically significant differences, indicating that national KPIs would misrepresent regional building stocks. Where no significant differences were found, regional datasets were aggregated to propose national KPIs. Improved demolition‑permit documentation would enhance KPI robustness, underscoring the need for standardised, higher quality data. Expanding datasets and validating the results against demolition outcomes will be essential to strengthen KPI applicability.

PRACTICE RELEVANCE

When can national KPIs serve as a reliable forecast of reusable building products from demolition? When must regional differences be considered? For products with limited regional variation, such as roofing felt and timber frameworks, national KPIs can inform circular-construction planning. In contrast, gypsum boards, clay roof tiles and certain window types show substantial regional differences, likely driven by construction traditions and documentation practices, making region-specific KPIs necessary. Until greater stability from further data collection is demonstrated, regional KPIs should remain the basis for quantifying products, with national indicators applied only where consistency is evident. To improve data quality, policymakers should promote harmonised pre‑demolition audits, standardised reporting and digital documentation. Practitioners can use KPIs in early‑stage planning, while municipalities could integrate them into permit processes and make the data publicly accessible to strengthen regional reuse capacity.

item.title: Climate change risk and decision-making
item.description:
Highlights

Climate change has created a wide range of uncertainties and risks that will strongly impact the built as well as the natural environment. There is a need to address these risks appropriately, effectively and to an applicable timetable at all levels of governance; and especially within those occupations and professions that invest in, develop, design, manage and regulate the built environment. This requires the development of new skills and understanding in the sector, including learning from other disciplines that are currently working on risk analysis, preparation and prioritisation, and who have already developed language, abilities and techniques to describe, categorise and quantify risk in order to make well-informed decisions and take necessary action. Climate change risk is a system problem that exhibits many features of interconnectedness and interdependency, requiring multidimensional analysis ranging across the spectrum from high-probability–low-impact risks to low-probability–high-impact ones. This editorial, referencing the learning described in the papers and commentaries in this special issue, calls on those within all areas of the sector to urgently map a way forward to establish responsibilities and responses for understanding, advising on and addressing climate risk to and resulting from the built environment as it varies across the planet. This will require changes to education, qualification, professional practice, and the information and tools available to practitioners. The relative lack of research and guidance on the subject within the field means this is a pressing task for the sector and a significant challenge to all involved.

item.title: Technologies of reconstruction
item.description:
Highlights

Post-disaster and post-conflict reconstruction have generated a substantial body of scholarly and professional knowledge, yet this knowledge remains dispersed across disciplines, institutions, professional practices and individual reconstruction episodes. Reconstruction policy operates within a large but fragmented knowledge environment. To examine the organisation of the field, this special issue considers the complexity of such an environment, characterised not only by the number of problems it encompasses but also by the relationships between separate processes and diverse actors operating across different spatial and temporal scales. The special issue confirms both the value and the limitations of disciplinary specialisation: increasingly sophisticated knowledge of particular reconstruction problems has not necessarily produced an integrated understanding of reconstruction as a whole. Rather than seeking unification through a universal model, a dialectical composition of different forms of knowledge is proposed within a common conceptual structure. Recovering an older meaning of technology as the systematic organisation of knowledge concerning practical action, it considers the possibility of a ‘technology of reconstruction’. It concludes by exploring how an open ontology of reconstruction, supported by computational methods and artificial intelligence, might enable accumulated empirical experience to become systematically comparable while preserving disciplinary difference and contextual specificity. The development of an internationally governed, open ontology of reconstruction is proposed: a shared framework for describing reconstruction processes, actors, resources, decisions, relationships and outcomes while preserving contextual differences. Existing recovery institutions could provide the organisational basis for developing and testing such a framework. The immediate policy priority is the knowledge infrastructure required to make accumulated reconstruction experience collectively usable.
